chunks: "The gain-bandwidth product is the product of an amplifier's gain and the bandwidth over which that gain is available.

For a typical voltage-feedback op-amp, the open-loop gain starts huge, around 10 to the 5 at DC, but there's a dominant pole at a very low frequency, maybe 10 hertz, and above that the gain rolls off at 20 decibels per decade.
Because it falls at exactly that rate, gain times frequency stays constant along the roll-off, and that constant is the GBW.
It's also the frequency where the open-loop gain hits 1, the unity-gain frequency.
So a 1 megahertz GBW op-amp has a gain of 100,000 at 10 hertz, 100 at 10 kilohertz and 1 at 1 megahertz. When you close the loop, you trade gain for bandwidth.
The closed-loop bandwidth is roughly GBW divided by the closed-loop (noise) gain.
A gain-of-10 amplifier built with a 1 megahertz op-amp has about 100 kilohertz bandwidth, and a gain-of-100 one has about 10 kilohertz.
So when I choose an op-amp I take the highest frequency I need, multiply by the gain, and then add margin, say 5 to 10 times, for gain accuracy and phase.
For example, gain of 50 at 200 kilohertz with 5% accuracy needs about 30 megahertz.
Two caveats: it only works like this for voltage-feedback amps, and slew rate is a separate large-signal limit."
